message.content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data
- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

No API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# Running an Off-Schedule Capture After Proving Nothing Was Missed

The weekly Big 12 forecast capture is specified to run on Wednesdays, and the 2026-09-30 slot was missed. On 2026-10-02 it was run on a Friday anyway, but only after establishing that the deviation cost nothing: no Big 12 games were played between 9/26 and 10/2, so no Week 5 result fell inside the gap. The last capture before this one was 9/23, and the run was justified on the explicit ground that a late capture loses nothing when no state changed in the interval.

## Key Points

- **The schedule exists to protect a property, not to be obeyed.** The Wednesday cadence exists so each capture is a genuine pre-game freeze; what matters is that no games resolved between the scheduled slot and the actual run, which was verified directly rather than assumed.
- **The deviation was argued before it was taken,** with the specific interval named (9/26 to 10/2) and the prior capture dated (9/23), so the reasoning is auditable later rather than appearing as an unexplained Friday entry in the log.
- **A data-integrity check accompanied the run:** 16 of 16 teams, 12 games each, no games appearing or vanishing — confirming the snapshot's shape before any comparison was drawn from it.
- **Grading was reported with its misses, not just its hits.** Week 4: correct winner in 6 of 8 games, with Baylor 23-13 over Colorado hitting the 10-point margin exactly; misses were Kansas State over Cincinnati (Cincinnati won 31-26) and West Virginia at 67% against Oklahoma State (Oklahoma State won 41-24, a 27-point miss).
- **The next slot was re-anchored to the schedule, not to the deviation:** Wednesday 10/7, Mac only, recorded in `docs/STATUS.md` rather than left in the session transcript.

## Details

The transferable judgment is that a cadence is a proxy for a condition, and when the condition can be checked directly the proxy becomes negotiable. For a pre-game forecast freeze the condition is that the capture precedes the games it forecasts — the property that [[connections/hindsight-leakage-and-pregame-freeze-capture]] identifies as the only thing making a retrodictive dataset trustworthy. A Wednesday slot is a convenient way to guarantee that property every week, but it is not the property itself. Checking that no Big 12 games were played in the 9/26–10/2 window establishes the condition held, which is strictly stronger evidence than "we ran on the scheduled day." The inverse case is the one that makes this discipline load-bearing rather than permissive: had any game resolved in the gap, the late capture would have been contaminated and the correct action would have been to record the slot as lost rather than fill it.

Pairing the off-schedule run with a shape check and an honest grading report is what keeps the deviation from quietly degrading the dataset. The 16-teams/12-games verification confirms the snapshot is comparable to its predecessors before any movement is computed from it, which matters because the most interesting outputs of the run were deltas: expected-win movers against the 9/23 baseline (Oklahoma State +1.86, UCF +1.57, Cincinnati +1.20, Utah +1.00 up; West Virginia −1.33, Kansas State −1.32, Colorado −1.06, Iowa State −1.03 down) and probability swings (Oklahoma State vs Kansas State in week 10 up 33 points to 58%, Houston vs Kansas State in week 6 up 25 points to 58%, Utah vs BYU in week 10 up 25 points to 63%). A delta against a structurally different snapshot would be meaningless, so the shape check is a precondition of the headline numbers rather than a formality. The Week 4 grading follows the same instinct in reverse: reporting the 27-point West Virginia miss alongside the exact Baylor margin hit resists the selective-reporting pressure analysed in [[concepts/forecast-slicing-on-own-output-bias]] and [[connections/report-the-gap-rather-than-the-fraction]].

Finally, the next capture was pinned back to Wednesday 10/7 and written into `docs/STATUS.md` rather than carried in memory, so the one-off deviation does not become the new cadence. The explicit Mac-only annotation is the machine-scoping constraint documented in [[concepts/machine-scoped-task-execution-rule]], and recording it in the project's own STATUS file is the placement discipline from [[connections/write-the-decision-where-each-consumer-will-look]] — the next reader arrives at the question by opening the project, not by searching session logs.

# Global Prompt and Hook Stack Audit (2026-09-29)

On 2026-09-29 the global prompt and hook stack was audited and repaired in a single pass: nine fixes were applied and pushed across four repos, cutting per-session startup context from roughly 17 KB to 5.7 KB while removing self-contradictory and machine-specific instructions. The user gave blanket authorization for the proposed changes rather than reviewing each one, and the work closed with a handoff at `~/Desktop/DEV/docs/handoffs/2026-09-29-prompt-audit.md`. On 2026-09-30 the audit's deliberately-deferred item — the uncleared error log — was resolved once its contents had root causes.

## Key Points

- **Error log summarized by type, not occurrence.** The startup error section now emits one line per error *type* instead of one per occurrence. This single change accounts for most of the ~17 KB → ~5.7 KB startup-context reduction, and it was also what surfaced four previously invisible error types (daily-backup ×6, perch-pull ×2, compiler-backlog ×3, and an adjudication run at 315k against a 250k token budget) that the first partial-log pass had missed.
- **A hook can neutralize a plugin's injected prompt text, but must re-apply itself.** `hooks/superpowers-quiet.mjs` strips the superpowers "MUST invoke / EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT" block at each session start. Because plugin updates overwrite plugin files, the hook re-applies the strip every session; one noisy session after any plugin update is expected. All superpowers skills remain available — only the imperative prompt block is removed.
- **Bans rewritten as goals; descriptions rewritten as instructions.** Both global instruction files were reworded from prohibitions to objectives, the session routine (pull + read STATUS at start, commit + push at end) was converted from a *description* of practice into an actual instruction, and an AGENTS.md contradiction between "output nothing" and "report errors" at startup was removed.
- **Machine-specific paths now enumerate both machines everywhere.** Vault, memory-folder, and CLI paths list both the Windows and macOS values in both machine templates plus `DEV/CLAUDE.md` and `RESEARCH.md`.
- **The error log is cleared only once its contents are explained, and only after a dated copy.** On 2026-09-29 and again the morning of 2026-09-30, `transcripts/.errors.log` was deliberately left alone — 14 KB of 9/23–9/28 failures were still unfixed, and clearing would have hidden them. Once the stack-doctor pass that day attributed the memsearch timeouts to a stopped Milvus container and the 9/27 flush failure to a usage limit, the log was cleared *after* saving a dated copy, so the next startup warning shows only new failures.
- **Trimming already-tight prose yields little.** Memory-index trimming returned only 8.4 KB → 7.7 KB against an estimate of "roughly halve," because most lines were already compressed. Structural changes (summarize by type) beat line-level editing.

## Details

The audit's most transferable result is a ranking of context-reduction tactics by yield. Rewriting the error log to summarize per error *type* collapsed a repetitive, unbounded section into a bounded one and delivered the bulk of the savings; hand-trimming the memory index recovered 0.7 KB against a predicted halving because the prose was already dense. The general lesson is that per-session context bloat usually lives in *repetition* — N occurrences of the same condition rendered N times — rather than in verbosity, so the first place to look is any section whose length scales with event count instead of with distinct state.

The error-summary rewrite also had a correctness payoff independent of size. The original pass read only part of the log and therefore missed four error types entirely; the new full-log summarizer found them. A truncating summarizer is worse than no summarizer in one specific way — it produces a short, confident-looking section that silently omits whole failure classes. The lifecycle of that log then demonstrates the complementary discipline: a warning log is a standing work queue, so clearing it is a claim that its contents are resolved. Holding it uncleared for two sessions while the failures were unexplained, then clearing it on 2026-09-30 only after each class had a root cause (Milvus container down; a usage-limit hit) and only after archiving a dated copy, preserves both properties — the next startup warning becomes a true signal about *new* failures, and nothing is actually destroyed. The dated copy is what makes clearing reversible, and therefore safe.

The `superpowers-quiet.mjs` hook establishes a pattern worth naming: a plugin that injects imperative prompt text can be muted at the consumer side without uninstalling it, by stripping the block at session start. The cost is that the fix is not durable in the plugin's own files, so the hook must re-assert itself each session — the same install-time-capture-goes-stale problem seen elsewhere in this environment, resolved here by refusing to capture at install time at all and re-deriving the desired state every session. Verification was deliberately pushed to the *next* session start rather than asserted at the end, because the fixes only take effect on a fresh read of `settings.json`. The Mac-side item could not be automated at all — the new "paths that differ" section in `machine.macos.md` must be copied by hand into the Mac's own unsynced `machine.md`.

# Two-Pass Documentation Verification of the Cross-Platform Claude Setup

On the evening of 2026-10-03, two consecutive read-only passes were run in Codex over another agent's cross-platform fixes to the Claude Code setup — `.claude/skills/status-report/SKILL.md`, `DEV/WORKFLOW.md`, `DEV/COMMANDS.md`, restored skill folders, `settings.json`, and the `command-centre` Tier A memory file. The first pass returned 3 VERIFIED / 2 PROBLEM / 1 UNSURE with an overall verdict of "not yet fully verified for both machines"; the second, after fixes landed, found four of five items RESOLVED and one still wrong. Both passes modified nothing.

## Key Points

- **Per-item verdicts plus an overall verdict, and a verdict vocabulary that admits ignorance.** VERIFIED / PROBLEM / **UNSURE** lets a blocked check be reported as blocked rather than guessed; Windows scheduler verification was UNSURE because `schtasks` failed and `Get-ScheduledTask` returned access denied without elevation, and the Git Bash dcg-hook execution test hit a Windows access-denied error.
- **Prose summaries drifted from the tables they describe.** `COMMANDS.md:21` said "two are off" while the nine-row A1 table actually broke down as 6 scheduled / 1 on-demand / 1 disabled / 1 pending shutdown — and remained wrong after the first round of fixes, making it the only item still open on the second pass.
- **"Pending shutdown" is a distinct state from "off."** Collapsing the two is what produced the miscount; the Mac command-centre launchd agent was still running, with `launchctl list | grep commandcentre` recorded in `project_command-centre.md:12` as the check.
- **A documented remedy can be destructive.** `WORKFLOW.md:217` recommended `git checkout -- settings.json`, which discards *all* unstaged settings edits instead of isolating the unwanted hook; it was replaced with targeted removal of the hook object.
- **Two factual claims in WORKFLOW.md were simply false and were corrected:** that global-memory is the "only thing" carrying memory between machines (the `.claude` repo tracks 308 memory `.md` files), and that the PDF probe works everywhere (requalified as Windows-tested / Mac-untested). A recipient mismatch was also reconciled — WORKFLOW.md:175 said Chris with Kenny cc'd, `status-report/SKILL.md:14` addressed both — resolving to Kenny Boyd + Chris Ruf.
- **The second pass stayed static by choice,** declining the optional Chrome curly-quote encoding test, and the undone check was recorded rather than treated as passed.

## Details

The notable property of this audit is that its findings are overwhelmingly about *documentation* rather than code, and that the documentation errors were the dangerous ones. A wrong `subprocess` encoding breaks loudly on the next run; a sentence claiming eight scheduled jobs "run on their own," a `kickstart` command offered for a ritual agent that STATUS records as disabled, and a "only thing carrying memory between machines" claim contradicted by 308 tracked files are all errors that an operator would act on confidently and be wrong. The destructive `git checkout -- settings.json` recommendation is the sharpest case: following the documented remedy would have discarded unrelated settings work while leaving the regenerating `dcg` hook untouched, converting a recurring annoyance into occasional data loss. Auditing a document for truth, rather than for presence, is therefore a distinct and necessary activity from auditing code.

The two-pass structure is what gives the result its force. The first pass produced a list of specific line-anchored claims; a separate agent applied fixes; the second pass re-read the same lines and reported four resolved and one not. That the single survivor was the prose job count is consistent with how these errors arise — it is derived state restated by hand, and a fix pass naturally gravitates to the items with concrete replacements while a count requires recounting from a table whose rows changed status. The second pass also surfaced the same-day `settings.json` recurrence evidence: a four-commit removed/restored/removed/restored history with the last restoration labeled "mac snapshot (closeout 2026-10-03)", which establishes recurrence while leaving the writing mechanism unidentified. Residuals were carried forward explicitly rather than closed: make `status-report` lines 83 and 85 shell-agnostic, fix the COMMANDS.md count, stop the Mac launchd agent, re-run the Windows scheduled-task check from an elevated session, and confirm that the Mac Command Centre archive script instructed at `project-triage/docs/STATUS.md:47` actually ran.

# Stale Hook-Failure Signals and the Archive-Hides-Open-Items Hazard

A 2026-10-03 Mac session set out to fix three session-start hook errors and found that two of them were already resolved. The `perch-pull` failure of 10/01 11:55 AM had been followed by a successful run the next afternoon at 4:35 PM (13,826 rows, newest test date 10/02, Google Drive copy to `athlete-snapshots/perch` succeeded), and the `manifest-unmanaged:42Analytics` backup error had been fixed independently by another session at 4:49 PM. The session's durable finding is a pair of rules: check the newest run's timestamp before rerunning a failed job, and treat archiving `.errors.log` as an act that silently removes still-open items from the session-start surface.

## Key Points

- **A session-start error banner is a record of a past failure, not a statement about current state.** The failing job may have succeeded on a later schedule; the newest run timestamp, not the error line, answers whether a rerun is needed.
- **Self-healing is a real disposition.** `perch-pull` recovered on its own next scheduled run, so the correct action was none at all — reruns of a job that already succeeded cost time and can duplicate work.
- **Archiving the error log suppresses unfixed items.** Another job moved `.errors.log` to `.errors.log.archived-2026-10-02` at 4:48 PM, carrying away three genuinely open items — `aios-audit` due, `memsearch-sync` index failure on the Windows laptop, and `daily-backup` / `repo-behind-blocked:global-memory` — which then stopped surfacing at session start despite being unresolved.
- **The archive therefore needs an explicit review hook.** The three suppressed items were carried forward into the next closeout by hand, because nothing else would raise them again.
- **Concurrent sessions and jobs race on this shared state.** One job archived the log before an approved edit landed, and a separate session fixed the manifest entry; both changed the world between the diagnosis and the intended action.

## Details

The staleness problem is structural rather than accidental. The session-start hook reports what the error log contains, and the error log is append-only escalation history — it records that a job failed at a moment in time and has no mechanism for retracting that line when a later run succeeds. So every banner read at session start is a claim about the past presented in the present tense, and acting on it without consulting the job's own most recent run is how a resolved failure turns into unnecessary remediation. The cheap check is always the same shape: find the newest run of the named job and read its outcome. Here that check converted a planned rerun into a no-op and produced positive evidence of health (row count, newest data date, successful Drive copy) rather than mere absence of a new error.

The archiving hazard runs in the opposite direction and is the more expensive of the two. Clearing or archiving the log is the right move once its contents are confirmed stale, which is exactly what happened earlier the same day for the resolved Docker/Milvus failure. But a blanket archive performed by an automated job cannot make that confirmation, so it removes resolved and unresolved entries alike, and the unresolved ones lose their only recurring channel to the operator. The three items lifted out on 10/02 at 4:48 PM are precisely the ones that needed to keep surfacing: an audit that was due, a cross-machine indexing failure, and a backup blocked by a repo being behind. Once archived, their continued existence depends entirely on someone having written them into a closeout note — which in this case someone did, with named verification commands (`grep MANIFEST ~/.claude/scripts/logs/daily-backup.log | tail -1` for the manifest fix, and a confirmation that the `repo-behind-blocked` condition cleared on the next 21:00 run). The general rule that emerges is that the archive step must be paired either with a confirmation that every entry is stale, or with an explicit carry-forward of the entries that are not.

# Applied Performance Digest: Delegated Build in Performance_Playbook

On 2026-10-04 the first chapter scaffold of the Applied Performance Digest was built in the `Performance_Playbook` repo by delegating a `/goal` prompt to a Fable subagent, after a parallel search established which source documents were actually current. The Digest is defined — in a prior handoff note rather than in the prompt — as a three-part artifact: a handbook, an operations manual, and NCAA technology items. Work was isolated in a git worktree on branch `digest-start`, surfaced as draft PR #1, and nothing was merged. Chapter 01 came in at 2,858 words against an 800-word minimum, carrying 27–28 unresolved `[CONFIRM: ...]` tags and five open decisions that gate a 10/23 ship date.

## Key Points

- **Four of five sources were settled before drafting.** The Baylor November 2025 `.docx` was adopted as the base because it is the newest copy, with the May 2024 PDF retained only for page references; Iowa's Sports Performance Assessment Manual and Clemson's material were used for format, structure, and ideas rather than content.
- **The fifth source was added only because a handoff note defined the scope.** `RunningTheRoom/docs/handoffs/2026-09-25-answers-self-audit-myelin-cleanup.md` names NCAA technology items as one of the Digest's three parts, so `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc` had to be added to the prompt — without it the outline would have omitted roughly a third of the deliverable.
- **The NCAA guide and forms A–E are linked, not rewritten,** and that repo was left unedited — a deliberate boundary between consuming a deliverable and absorbing it.
- **Two internal Baylor documents imply two live ForceDecks app versions.** The "Revised Force Plate Testing V3" protocol and the Operations Guide use different ForceDecks button names, which is a tooling-drift signal discovered by reading documentation rather than devices.
- **Five decisions gate the 10/23 chapter-01 ship:** whether V3 (3 reps, hands on hips) is live and which ForceDecks app version is on the device; soft landing (V3) versus stiff landing (Iowa), where soft matches practice but breaks comparability of landing-force metrics; who the named daily user and co-owner is, with a 30-day check around 11/22; whether VALD Hub → Kitman Labs → department DB moves by API or CSV and for which sports; and whether chapter 01 retires the Operations Guide's ForceDecks section at ship.

## Details

The session's structure is worth separating from its content: a source-currency investigation ran first, a delegated drafting run second, and an independent verification pass third. The investigation mattered more than it looked like it would. No Iowa file is literally a "playbook"; the Iowa source is the Sports Performance Assessment Manual, which exists as near-identical copies dated 2017, a 2021 draft, and a May 2024 PDF — and the "May 2024" file proved textually identical to the 2017-11-06 copy, same 27 pages, same 5,085 words, same 2017 creation metadata. On the Baylor side the November 2025 `.docx` is the only copy newer than the May 2024 PDF and is 97.5% identical to it at word level, differing in the table of contents, one table position, and one phrase. The operational consequence is that the February 2026 gap analysis still applies in full, because nothing of substance changed between the two Baylor copies.

The open items divide cleanly into protocol questions and ownership questions. The protocol questions are genuinely substantive trade-offs rather than editorial choices: a soft landing matches how athletes actually land in practice, but switching away from the stiff-landing convention breaks comparability of landing-force metrics against historical data — the same baseline-continuity tension that recurs across Baylor's force-plate work. The ownership questions determine whether the chapter is a document or a practice: a named daily user with a 30-day check converts the chapter from prose into something with an owner and a review date, and the decision about whether chapter 01 retires the Operations Guide's ForceDecks section determines whether the Digest *replaces* existing documentation or quietly duplicates it. Two naming and provenance loose ends remain: the department is called "Athletics Performance" in the guide and "Athletic Performance" in the Digest term list, and an "AP Assessment Manual V12" named in Flint provenance notes was not found on disk or on Drive. An `articulation` pass on chapter 01 is logged in STATUS Next before it can go to v1.0, and the worktree is to be removed with `git worktree remove .claude/worktrees/digest-start` after PR #1 merges.

# Windows Laptop Backup Failure and RECOVERY-INVENTORY.md

On 2026-09-14 a `RECOVERY-INVENTORY.md` commit arriving from the Windows laptop revealed that the machine had **no working backup at all**. Roughly 15 GB exists in a single copy only — `SportScienceResearchRepo` (4.37 GB), `Football` (2.94 GB), `Risk_Stratification_Engine` (1.80 GB), `ForcePlate_DecisionSystem` (1.69 GB), and the `~/.codex` history. Everything else — all 131 repos, `~/.claude`, skills, global memory, and Google Drive documents — is safe. The failure had three independent root causes, all of them artifacts of the Mac migration.

## Key Points

- **Nine KeystoneOS Windows scheduled tasks are Disabled** — switched off during the move to the Mac and never restored. They report their disabled state accurately; nothing ever escalated it.
- **Two replacement tasks were registered with no trigger.** A triggerless task shows `Ready` indefinitely and will never fire — the healthiest-looking possible state for a job that does nothing.
- **The Windows backup manifest is the Mac's manifest.** It carries `/Volumes/CRASHBOX` and `/Users/kristinarash/...` paths, with its last state written 2026-08-14 at status ERROR. `~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1` had likewise been overwritten by the Mac version (rsync + Mac paths) on 2026-08-05; the original is frozen at `daily-backup.ps1.win-orig`.
- **`backup_dev.ps1` was changed from `/MIR` to `/E`.** Mirroring propagates accidental deletions into the backup, which converts the backup into a second copy of a mistake rather than a recovery path. (`backup_ai_sessions.ps1` was already `/E`.)
- **Two deliberate non-actions:** the backup scripts stay in `DEV\_INBOX\` because the registered scheduled task points there, and the nine disabled tasks are *not* re-enabled because the script they invoke is now the Mac's.

## Details

What makes this a distinct failure rather than another manifest-drift instance is that every layer reported truthfully and none of them reported the operational fact. A disabled task is disabled; a triggerless task is genuinely ready; a manifest containing Mac paths is a syntactically valid manifest. The only signal that would have surfaced the problem is the one nobody was checking: whether bytes actually landed in Google Drive. This is the same scope mismatch catalogued in [[connections/status-field-scope-narrower-than-the-question]], where `launchctl list` reports only the last *scheduled* run — the field answers a narrower predicate than the operator's question and is therefore silent about the gap. The recovery report's own conclusion states the rule directly: verification must confirm bytes at the destination, not that the task looks healthy.

The three causes also share a single origin. Tasks disabled "during the Mac move," a manifest overwritten with Mac paths on 08-14, a `daily-backup.ps1` overwritten on 08-05 — the migration edited the Windows machine's automation surface as a side effect of syncing shared files, and nothing on the Windows side was left running to notice. This extends the pattern in [[connections/windows-defaults-outlive-the-windows-machine]] in the opposite direction: that article covers Windows assumptions surviving onto the Mac, whereas here Mac-shaped configuration flowed back onto Windows through the same shared repositories. Bidirectional sync between two machines with platform-specific automation means any file that encodes host facts — paths, mount points, shell dialects — is a collision waiting to happen, which is why the new `~/.claude/scripts/backup-manifest.windows.json` was created as a *separate* file rather than a re-edit of the shared one.

The `/MIR` → `/E` change deserves isolation as policy. Robocopy's `/MIR` makes the destination an exact mirror of the source, which means a local deletion is faithfully reproduced in the backup at the next run — the backup is then a copy of the current state rather than a record of history. `/E` copies without deleting, accepting stale files in exchange for never propagating a loss. The trade-off resolves the same way as the append-only forecast log in [[concepts/cross-machine-conflict-file-triage]]: when the artifact's value is that it holds something the source might no longer have, the correct verb is never "make identical."

# Vendored Skill Hand-Install Pattern (~/.agents/skills → Claude + Codex)

On 2026-09-04, the `davidondrej/skills` GitHub repository (58 skills) was vetted against the existing environment and five skills were installed by hand after the official `npx skills add` installer was blocked by the auto-mode permission classifier. The session established a working install shape — vendor directory plus two layers of symlink — verified it empirically rather than by assumption, and documented a real cost of the manual route: hand-installed skills are invisible to the upstream lockfile and therefore to `skills update`.

## Key Points

- **53 of 58 skills rejected, with reasons by category:** duplicates of already-installed capability (superpowers, session-handoff, CreateSkill, codex plugin, launchd), dependence on tools absent from this machine (bb, cmux, Herdr, Pi, Cursor, Postgres), a paid DeepAPI key requirement (`risky-changes` and all ten `research-and-web` skills), and hardcoding of the author's own name (`file-tree`, `stop-overthinking`, `short`, `remind`).
- **Five installed, taking the count 151 → 156:** `persistent-localhost` (runs dev servers as launchd jobs, replacing `&`/`nohup`), `anti-sleep` (`caffeinate` for long or overnight runs), and three slash-only skills — `/decisions`, `/before-building`, `/next-decision`.
- **`global-agent-guardrails` was skipped for a concrete conflict,** not redundancy alone: `dcg` already covers the ground, and the skill's denylist blocks `security find-generic-password`, which the Fireflies key read depends on.
- **The working install shape:** copy `SKILL.md` plus `scripts/` and `agents/` into `~/.agents/skills/<name>/`, `chmod +x` the scripts, symlink *relatively* into `~/.claude/skills/<name>`, then symlink `~/.codex/skills/<name>` at `~/.claude/skills/<name>` — every Codex entry points at the Claude path, not at `~/.agents/skills` directly.
- **Hand-installed skills are absent from `~/.agents/.skill-lock.json`,** so `skills update` will not see them. Registering them retroactively is possible by running the official installer behind a `!` prefix to bypass the classifier; it may simply report "already installed."
- **Both installs were tested, not assumed:** `persistent-localhost` served a real HTTP 200 on port 5199 and stopped cleanly; `anti-sleep` reached `ASSERTIONS=active` and stopped leaving no stray plists.

## Details

The vetting ratio — 5 accepted out of 58 — is the substantive finding, and the four rejection categories are reusable as a triage rubric for any third-party skill bundle. Duplication is the largest bucket and the cheapest to check, since an existing capability makes the new skill pure listing overhead against the description budget documented in [[concepts/skill-description-budget-ceiling]]. Missing-dependency and paid-key rejections are hard constraints discoverable by reading the skill body. The author-name-hardcoding category is the least obvious and the most instructive: a skill written for personal use may embed its author's identity in prompts or paths, which makes it silently wrong rather than broken when installed elsewhere. The `global-agent-guardrails` rejection is a fifth, sharper category — active interference, where the skill's denylist would have broken an unrelated working integration (the Fireflies keychain read). That is a case where "we already have coverage" understates the reason to decline.

The symlink topology is worth stating precisely because it is not the obvious arrangement. The canonical files live once in `~/.agents/skills/<name>/`; `~/.claude/skills/<name>` is a *relative* symlink into that directory; and `~/.codex/skills/<name>` symlinks to the Claude path rather than to the vendor path. Routing Codex through Claude rather than pointing both harnesses at the vendor directory means the Claude path is the single indirection point — moving or replacing the underlying skill requires updating one link, not two. The insistence on a relative link for the Claude leg matters given this environment's history with committed symlinks: absolute links that encode a home directory are exactly what broke during the Windows→Mac migration described in [[concepts/committed-symlink-repo-landmine]].

The lockfile gap is the genuine cost of hand-installing and should be recorded wherever the install is documented. `~/.agents/.skill-lock.json` is the manifest `skills update` consults, so a skill installed outside the installer is functionally present but permanently unmanaged — it will never receive an upstream fix. This is the same silent-omission shape as a backup manifest that does not list a folder: every managed item reports success, and the unmanaged item is invisible precisely because nothing knows to look for it. The offered remedy (re-running the official installer behind `!` purely to register the entries) resolves the bookkeeping without repeating the file operations. A final procedural note from the same session: two prior claims recorded in `project_vendored-skill-install.md` were disproven during this work and corrected in Tier A memory, which is the correct disposition for memory that testing contradicts.

# Install-Time Environment Capture Rots Silently

The memory compiler's Tier C failure (2026-06-13) and the memsearch outage (2026-06-11, generalized 2026-06-17) look like unrelated incidents — one a dependency version skew, the other a broken Windows shim. They are the same failure: a tool froze a piece of its host environment at install time, the host moved, and the frozen copy became a lie. Neither tool changed. Neither configuration changed. Both stopped working.

## Key Points

- **The captured artifact differs; the mechanism does not.** memsearch.exe embedded an absolute Python interpreter path; a `.venv`'s `pyvenv.cfg` embedded `home = C:\Python314`; the memory compiler's `uv` venv pinned `claude-agent-sdk==0.1.56` and thereby a bundled Claude Code CLI at 2.1.92. Each is a snapshot of the host taken once, at install, and never refreshed.
- **The host moves on its own schedule.** Python was migrated to a new path; Claude Code auto-updated 85 releases ahead. Neither event was initiated as a change to the dependent tool, which is exactly why the resulting failure is unattributed — nothing in the failing tool's history explains it.
- **Both fail at startup, before producing a diagnostic.** `flush.py` exited non-zero immediately (100% FLUSH_ERROR); memsearch.exe errored about an interpreter path. Startup-time death means the failure surfaces as an exit code rather than a message, which is why both were initially misread as flaky hooks rather than broken environments.
- **The fix is always "rebuild the capture," never "fix the environment."** `uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync`; reinstall memsearch into the new Python; rebuild the venv. Adjusting PATH or settings cannot help — the stale value lives inside the tool, not around it.
- **Diagnose by inspecting metadata, not by running the artifact.** The compiler note's explicit caution — do not invoke the bundled `claude.exe` to check its version, because it spawns a real nested agent session — is the sharp form of a general rule: read `uv pip show`, read `pyvenv.cfg`, don't execute the thing you suspect is broken.

## Details

What makes this class distinct from the neighbouring Windows-environment failures already documented in this vault is *where the stale value lives*. In [[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]], a correct new value exists in the registry and merely hasn't reached running processes; in [[concepts/windows-task-scheduler-path-config]], the spawning system never supplied the user's PATH at all. Both are problems of the environment *surrounding* the process, and both are fixed from outside it. Install-time capture inverts this: the surrounding environment is entirely correct — the new Python is installed and on PATH, the current Claude Code CLI is present and functional — and the tool still fails, because it is consulting a private copy of a fact that expired. This inversion is what makes the diagnosis counterintuitive. The instinct on a path error is to check PATH, and PATH will look fine. The memsearch note names the resulting fingerprint precisely: the binary exists, its location is on PATH, and it still errors about interpreter paths.

The two incidents also demonstrate the same containment property, which is worth stating because it is what makes these failures survivable rather than catastrophic. The compiler's Tier C death did not touch Tier B, because `transcript-capture.js` has no `claude-agent-sdk` dependency and therefore no captured copy of anything — 24 days of continuous logs proved the independence empirically (see [[connections/memory-compiler-tier-independence-under-failure]]). Symmetrically, memsearch's ETIMEDOUT contention is explicitly non-fatal and does not corrupt the index. In both systems, the component that froze a host fact is the component that broke, and the components that resolve their dependencies at call time kept running. That is a design lever, not just an observation: the fewer host facts a component snapshots, the fewer ways an unrelated upgrade can kill it. Where snapshotting is unavoidable — a compiled shim, a venv, a pinned SDK — the corresponding obligation is a post-upgrade check, because nothing in the tool will announce that its copy went stale.

A practical corollary follows for hook-installed tooling specifically. Hooks fire unattended, their stderr often goes nowhere, and a startup-time exit is indistinguishable from a no-op — the memsearch note records one silent `exit 1` with no surviving diagnostic output, cause unknown to this day. So the maintenance trigger cannot be "wait for an error message." It has to be event-driven on the *host* side: after any Python migration or Claude Code auto-update, enumerate the tools holding captured copies (patched binaries, venvs, pinned SDK bundles) and rebuild them, then run a verification flush before trusting normal operation to have resumed.

# Filename Dates Lie: Establishing Document Currency Before Reuse

Before drafting the Applied Performance Digest on 2026-10-04, a parallel search established which of several candidate source documents were actually current. Two findings inverted the apparent chronology. Iowa's Sports Performance Assessment Manual exists as near-identical copies labelled 2017, a 2021 draft, and a May 2024 PDF — but the "May 2024" file is textually identical to the 2017-11-06 copy: same 27 pages, same 5,085 words, same 2017 creation metadata. And Baylor's November 2025 `.docx`, the only copy newer than its own May 2024 PDF, proved 97.5% identical to it at word level, differing only in the table of contents, one table position, and one phrase.

## Key Points

- **A filename or distribution date records when a copy was circulated, not when its content was written.** The Iowa "May 2024" PDF is 2017 text by metadata and by word-for-word comparison.
- **Three independent signals agreed:** page count, word count, and PDF creation metadata all placed the content in 2017, which is what made the conclusion safe to act on.
- **Near-identity is as important a finding as staleness.** Baylor's Nov 2025 and May 2024 copies being 97.5% identical means the February 2026 gap analysis built against the older copy still applies in full — no re-analysis needed.
- **The currency check determined the base document.** The Nov 2025 `.docx` was adopted as the content base because it is newest, with the PDF kept only for page references.
- **The search also corrected a naming assumption:** no Iowa file is literally a "playbook"; the source is the Sports Performance Assessment Manual, so the remembered name would not have found it.

## Details

The cost of skipping a currency check is asymmetric and silent. Treating the Iowa "May 2024" PDF as 2024 material would have imported seven-year-old protocol conventions as current peer practice, with the file's own name as the apparent warrant. Conversely, treating the Baylor November 2025 copy as substantially new would have triggered an unnecessary re-run of the February 2026 gap analysis — work that the 97.5% diff proved pointless. Both errors are invisible from the file listing, which is the only view most source-selection decisions get. What made them visible was cheap, mechanical comparison: diff the two copies, count words, read the PDF's creation metadata.

This generalizes a pattern recorded elsewhere in the knowledge base about reading metadata rather than running or trusting an artifact — the same move that diagnosed a stale install-time environment capture by inspecting its recorded version instead of executing it. Here the artifact is prose rather than a virtualenv, but the discipline is identical: the object's self-description is evidence, and it frequently contradicts the label someone attached to the container. The practical procedure is short enough to make routine before any document reuse — enumerate every copy, compare them pairwise, read creation metadata, and only then decide which is the base and what the others are good for. A related loose end from the same session shows the limit of the method: "AP Assessment Manual V12" is named in Flint provenance notes but was not found on disk or on Drive, so a document can be cited by a name that resolves to nothing at all.

# Instrumenting a Silently Failing Scheduled Task

A scheduled job that succeeds when run by hand but dies seconds after the scheduler launches it supplies no diagnostic surface, and on 2026-10-01 that situation was addressed by adding instrumentation rather than by guessing at causes. The recall-eval task, queued to run after the overnight vault index, terminated within roughly 7 seconds; it ran correctly when invoked manually, encoding was ruled out, a suspected credential cause was retracted, and Task Scheduler history is disabled on the laptop. The chosen next step was to add output logging so the next scheduled run — Sunday at 02:00 — captures the real error.

## Key Points

- **Works-by-hand plus fails-on-schedule localizes the fault to the launch environment,** not to the program: the difference between the two invocations is the spawning context, not the code.
- **The diagnostic surface was absent on three fronts simultaneously:** the task emitted no captured output, Task Scheduler history was disabled, and the ~7-second exit left no artifact to inspect.
- **Candidate causes were eliminated rather than assumed.** Encoding was ruled out, and the plausible `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` explanation was investigated and retracted once a live call confirmed the credential worked.
- **The fix is instrumentation, with the failure allowed to recur.** Adding output logging and letting Sunday's scheduled run fail again is cheaper and more informative than a blind workaround, and the recurrence is expected ("the failure will likely recur otherwise").
- **A secondary artifact gap was logged as optional follow-up:** the 02:49 `post-vault-index` rows that never got written to `~/.claude/audits/recall-eval/LATEST.md`, left unopened.

## Details

The asymmetry between a manual run and a scheduled run is itself the primary clue. When identical code succeeds interactively and dies under the scheduler, the variable is the environment the scheduler hands the process: its working directory, its PATH, its user context, its environment variables, and whether a dependency it needs is up at that hour. This project's history supplies several precedents — Task Scheduler's minimal spawn environment requiring full absolute executable paths, and a process's environment being fixed at launch so later registry writes are invisible to it. A ~7-second exit is consistent with that family: long enough to start, short enough to fail before doing real work, which is the signature of a resolution or startup failure rather than a timeout or a logic error. But "consistent with" is not a diagnosis, and the session deliberately stopped short of asserting one.

That restraint matters because a plausible cause had already been wrongly asserted and then withdrawn. The `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` "saved EMPTY" note looked like an explanation, and investigating it properly showed the credential was present in a gitignored file and functional on a live call — removing the candidate and leaving the failure genuinely open. Having lost one false explanation, adopting a second guess would risk the same outcome at greater cost. Instrumentation sidesteps the problem entirely: capture the task's stdout and stderr, let the next scheduled run fail, and read the actual error. The cost is one more week of a non-functional weekly eval; the benefit is that the next failure is self-explaining. The same reasoning covers the unwritten `post-vault-index` rows in `LATEST.md` — recorded as an optional item to investigate rather than reconstructed by inference, since the file itself may hold the partial evidence once opened.

# Connection: A Settings-Based Fix Is Not a Fix When the Setting Is Volatile

## The Connection

The 2026-10-02 Power Query repair rejected a working remedy. Toggling the workbook's "Ignore privacy levels" option demonstrably stopped the `Formula.Firewall` error, yet it was refused as the fix because the setting had already reverted once — plausibly during a save or a rename — and because a user's *global* Excel privacy preference can override it on any other machine. The adopted answer collapsed five queries into one self-contained `Kinexon Master`, eliminating the cross-source composition the firewall reacts to, so that no setting needs to hold ([[concepts/power-query-firewall-structural-fix]]).

The same reasoning already governs several items in this environment. The `superpowers-quiet.mjs` hook does not edit plugin files once and trust the edit to persist; it re-derives the stripped state at every session start, because plugin updates overwrite them ([[concepts/global-prompt-stack-audit]]). The duplicate `dcg` `PreToolUse` entry was repaired not by maintaining per-machine settings but by removing the machine-specific path so the single remaining entry no-ops where it does not apply ([[concepts/cross-platform-settings-json-hook-duplication]]) — a removal repeated in this same day's dev-mods session. And a `setx` write to the registry is real but invisible to every already-running process, so the configuration is only as durable as the next restart ([[concepts/windows-setx-env-propagation]]).

## Key Insight

The test for whether a configuration-level remedy counts as a fix is not "does it stop the symptom" but "what resets it, and who else can override it." A per-workbook flag that a save or rename can clear, a plugin file that the next update overwrites, a hook path valid on exactly one host, and an environment variable invisible to running processes all pass the symptom test and fail the durability test. Each has a hostile party that is part of normal operation rather than an exception — the file lifecycle, the package manager, the second machine, the already-launched process.

Three distinct responses follow, and which one applies depends on what owns the volatility. When the triggering condition can be removed, remove it: one self-contained query gives the firewall nothing to evaluate, and that is strictly better than configuring the firewall to look away. When the state cannot be made durable, stop trying to capture it and re-derive it on every run, as the quiet hook does. When the reference itself is the problem, make it host-agnostic so one artifact is correct everywhere rather than correct once. The failure mode common to all three is that a settings-based fix is *silent* when it lapses — the workbook simply errors again on the next open, the plugin simply shouts again after an update — so the lapse is discovered by the user hitting the original bug rather than by anything reporting a regression.

## Evidence

- 2026-10-02: the Box copy of `VB_Revised.xlsx` held the identical query code as the 9/30 fix; only the workbook-level privacy flag had reverted, most likely during the 9:08 save or the 9:10 rename. The stated lesson: "structural fixes beat settings-based workarounds for files shared across machines," with the setting retained as belt-and-suspenders only.
- 2026-10-02: the `dcg` `PreToolUse` hook in `~/.claude/settings.json` still carried a hard-coded Mac path; removing it left one cross-platform entry that no-ops on Windows.
- 2026-09-29: `hooks/superpowers-quiet.mjs` re-applies its strip every session because plugin updates overwrite plugin files; one noisy session after any update is expected and accepted.
- 2026-10-02: `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS` required opening a new terminal before Claude Code could see it — the registry write was immediate, the running process's view was not.

# Project Memory Index Size as a Recurring Per-Session Cost

On 2026-09-30 a `doctor-plus` context audit found the project memory index had grown to roughly 8,200 characters — a cost paid at the start of every session, because the index is auto-loaded rather than retrieved on demand. The index was trimmed from 8,162 to 5,549 characters (~30% smaller) by rewriting each line to state only *when to open* the file it points at, leaving all dates, counts, and error text inside the memory files themselves. All 56 links were verified after the rewrite.

## Key Points

- **The index is always-loaded, so its size is a standing tax**, not a one-time storage cost; growth that would be unremarkable in a retrievable file is expensive here.
- **The durable fix is a line-format rule, not a one-off cut:** each index line states only the condition under which a reader should open the target file. Details belong in the target.
- **Trim measured 8,162 → 5,549 chars (~30%)** with no pointer removed — the reduction came entirely from moving content down a tier, not from dropping entries.
- **All 56 links were verified after the rewrite**, because a reformatting pass over a pointer file is exactly the operation most likely to produce a dangling pointer.
- **This is the same lever applied one layer out** from the Tier A index trim (15 → 10 files) and the repeated `MEMORY.md` cap trims, and it has the same failure mode: without a format rule, the file re-grows.

## Details

A pointer index occupies an unusual position in the memory architecture: it is the mechanism by which content becomes retrievable rather than resident, and yet it is itself resident. That makes it the one file where restating a fact is doubly expensive — the fact is paid for in the index every session *and* stored again in the file the index points at. The observed growth to ~8,200 characters came from exactly that duplication: index lines had accumulated dates, counts, and error strings that already existed in their targets, apparently on the reasoning that a richer index saves a read. The trim rejects that trade, because a read is conditional and cheap while the index is unconditional.

Encoding the fix as a line *format* rather than a size target is what distinguishes this pass from the earlier wording-compression attempts on `MEMORY.md` catalogued in [[concepts/memory-cap-relief-by-migration-not-deletion]]. Compression shortens prose and buys bytes that are immediately re-spent; a format rule ("state when to open this file, nothing else") answers the question that produces the growth in the first place, so the next person adding an entry knows what not to write. It also makes the index auditable: a line containing a date or a count is visibly out of format and can be fixed without a judgment call about whether it is worth its bytes. This is the same move as recording a mechanism instead of a magic number in [[connections/document-the-mechanism-not-the-magic-number]] — the abstraction level of the recorded content is chosen to match how stable that content is.

The link verification step matters because a bulk reformat is precisely the operation that silently breaks pointers. Fifty-six links rewritten by hand or by pattern is fifty-six chances to mistype a target, and a broken index entry is worse than a verbose one: a verbose entry costs tokens, while a dangling one resolves to nothing and makes a real memory file invisible. Verifying after the pass rather than trusting the edit is the same discipline as re-running the doctor to confirm a cap fix, and the same hazard as the stale-pointer class described in [[connections/a-stale-pointer-resolves-cleanly-to-the-wrong-answer]].

# Memory Recall Evaluation Harness (30-Question Retrieval Benchmark)

The recall-eval harness is a scheduled benchmark that scores competing memory-retrieval methods against a fixed 30-question set, writing results to `~/.claude/audits/recall-eval/LATEST.md`. On 2026-10-01 a manual run against a freshly built vault index produced the first fully-scoreable comparison of four methods, and its numbers were used to adjudicate whether the Docker/Milvus-backed memsearch stack should be retired in favor of a cheaper alternative. The harness exists precisely so that a retrieval-infrastructure decision is settled by measurement rather than by cost intuition.

## Key Points

- **Four methods, 30 questions (2026-10-01 run):** memsearch 29/30 hit@5, 15 hit@1, 5.7 s; fts5 + Jev 27/30, 19 hit@1, 0.4 s; plain fts5 25/30, 20 hit@1, 5 ms; `rg` 23/30, 11 hit@1, 111 ms. Coverage was 14/14 Tier A notes and 12/13 vault notes.
- **Pre-registered retirement rule:** memsearch is retired only if a cheaper method comes within 1 hit@5. fts5+Jev trails by 2, so the rule did not fire and the Docker/Milvus stack was kept.
- **Recall and ranking diverge.** memsearch wins hit@5 but loses hit@1 (15 vs plain fts5's 20) — it is better at *finding* the right note than at *ranking* it first. A single headline metric would have hidden this.
- **Indexing the vault changed the verdict's availability, not just its value.** Before the overnight index, memsearch was unscoreable; after it (started 22:30, finished 02:49, 259 minutes, 8,302 chunks) it became the best method on recall.
- **The scheduled run failed silently and is not yet diagnosed.** The eval task queued after the index died within ~7 seconds, runs fine by hand, and Task Scheduler history is disabled on the laptop — so the fix is to add output logging to the task before the next Sunday 02:00 run rather than to guess at a cause.

## Details

The harness's value on 2026-10-01 came less from any single score than from the structure it imposed on a decision. The question on the table — keep a Docker/Milvus semantic-search stack or drop to SQLite FTS5 — is exactly the kind of question that gets answered by vibes: the cheaper method is dramatically faster (5 ms versus 5.7 s) and carries no container dependency, and a stopped Milvus container had already caused days of memsearch timeouts (see [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]]). A pre-registered bar — "within 1 hit@5" — prevented that convenience from deciding the matter. fts5+Jev landed 2 behind, the rule did not fire, and memsearch stayed. This is the same discipline as writing a pass bar before running a model (see [[concepts/pre-registered-pass-bar]]) and the same demand that a model be justified by the failure of the strongest cheap alternative rather than any alternative (see [[connections/measured-baseline-before-model-adoption]]) — here the cheap alternatives were genuinely strong, and the rule was honored in the direction of keeping the expensive tool.

The hit@5 / hit@1 split is the run's most useful substantive finding. Reporting both metrics exposed a behavioral difference the aggregate obscures: memsearch retrieves the relevant note into the top five almost always (29/30) but places it first only half the time (15/30), while plain FTS5 misses more often (25/30) yet ranks precisely when it hits (20/30). Characterized plainly, memsearch is a recall instrument and lexical search is a precision instrument, which argues for using them for different jobs rather than picking one winner. It also means any future retirement test must keep reporting both numbers, since a method that matched memsearch on hit@5 while beating it on hit@1 would be a strict improvement, whereas one that matched on hit@5 alone would be a lateral move.

Two operational lessons attach to the run. First, the overnight index's 259-minute duration confirms that full-library embedding is an hours-scale job belonging to a scheduled task, consistent with the earlier relocation of the heavy reindex into the nightly backup. Second, the eval task's ~7-second death is currently uninformative: it reproduces only under the scheduler, the obvious candidate causes (encoding, a missing API key) were ruled out, and the scheduler's own history is disabled. The chosen response was not a workaround but an instrumentation change — add output logging so the next scheduled failure captures a real error — because an unlogged scheduled job that works by hand supplies no diagnostic surface at all.

---
title: "A Zero-Change Capture Signals Source Ingest Lag, Not a Capture Bug"
aliases: [all 16 teams 0 change, cfbvictorymodel.com has not ingested, games-played cross-check, ESPN schedule API cross-check, forecast capture ecae190, pre-ASU forecasts safe in 10-02 capture]
tags: [cfb, forecasting, verification, data-integrity, workflow, methodology]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-10-07.md"

updated: 2026-10-10
